DETAILED ACTION
This Non-Final action is responsive to the application and IDS filed 8/6/2021.
In the application Claims 1-10, 12, 16, 20-21 and 23-28 are pending. Claims 11, 13-15, 17-19, 22 and 29-37 are canceled. Claims 1 and 16 are the independent claims.
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 8/6/2021 has been entered, and considered by the examiner.
Priority
Acknowledgement is made to applicant’s claim for priority to PCT/CA2020/050163 filed 2/7/2020 which claims foreign priority to provisional application 62/802876, filed 2/8/2019.
Drawings
The Drawings filed on 8/6/2021 have been approved.
Claim Objections
Claim 10 is objected to because of the following minor informalities:  The claim recites “…is one or a slide and a slide spacer.” Which may have been intended to recite “…is one of a slide and a slide spacer”. Appropriate corrections are required.
Specification
8.	Applicant is reminded of the proper language and format for an abstract of the disclosure.
The abstract should be in narrative form and generally limited to a single paragraph on a separate sheet within the range of 50 to 150 words in length. The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether there is a need for consulting the full patent text for details.
The language should be clear and concise and should not repeat information given in the title. It should avoid using phrases which can be implied, such as, “The disclosure concerns,” “The disclosure defined by this invention,” “The disclosure describes,” etc.  In addition, the form and legal phraseology often used in patent claims, such as “means” and “said,” should be avoided.
7.	The abstract is objected to because it recites implied phrases such as “Systems, devices and methods for assembling a piece of furniture are described herein.”. Appropriate corrections are required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
9.	Claims 1-10 and 12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Chen (U.S. 4,613,942, filed Oct. 22, 1984) in view of Shinozaki (U.S. 9,649,790, filed Nov. 30, 2012) further in view of Ross (NPL- IkeaBot: An Autonomous Multi-Robot Coordinated Furniture Assembly System, published May 2013, pgs. 855-862).
Regarding Independent claim 1, Chen discloses A robot for assembling a piece of furniture, the robot comprising:
a base (see fig.1, numeral 18 & col. 2, lines 45-65, discloses robot base comprising control mechanism);
a robotic arm coupled to the base at a first end of the robotic arm (see fig.1, numeral 19 & col. 2, lines 45-65, discloses a robot arm);
a multi-functional robotic head coupled to the robotic arm at a second end of the robotic arm, the multi-functional robotic head comprising: a camera configured to scan a barcode positioned on a part presented to the robot, the barcode providing instructions to the robot for attaching one or more hardware components to the part to assemble the piece of furniture (see fig.1, numeral 14 & col. 2, lines 45-65, discloses a camera for obtaining and processing a coded indica image on a part within its field of vision. Further supporting use of a bar code for the indica in col. 4, lines 35-67. The part is then used to perform an assembly operation by the robot arm has determined by the indica outlined in col. 3, lines 25-35 & abstract);
a first gripping mechanism configured to grip a first hardware component, the first hardware component being manoeuvred by the robotic arm to a first position to be attached to the part (see fig. 1 numeral 20, col. 2, lines 50-55 & col. 3, lines 43-50, discloses a gripping mechanism has a robot manipulator used to grip a hardware component such as wrench 11. Further describing in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached);
a first attachment mechanism configured to attach the first hardware component to the part at the first position via a fastener to assemble the piece of furniture (see col. 5, lines 5-20, discloses parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached thereby applying fasteners for assembly); and
a computing unit in communication with the robotic arm and the multi-functional robotic head, the computing unit configured to receive the instructions from the camera and to control the robotic arm and the multi-functional robotic head to assemble the piece of furniture (see fig. 1 & col. 5, lines 5-20, discloses using a computer that communicates with the robotic arm and manipulator to receive instructions from the camera that obtained the indica image that is decoded to provide assemble instruction to the robot). Chen discloses obtaining robot assembly operation instructions based on captured indica placed on a part. He further mentions in col. 2, lines 65-67 the application of adhesives for attaching the indica, but fails to teach the robot applying any adhesive to furniture parts.
Shinozaki discloses:
a first applicator mechanism configured to apply an adhesive to the part (see abstract, discloses application of a curing adhesive to a region of an article using a robot); Shinozaki fails to teach any assembly of furniture parts using the robot. Ross discloses that applying Autonomous robots for the purpose of furniture parts assembly is well known (see pg. 855, paragraphs 1-4). It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented known techniques for applying adhesive for furniture assembly using the robot, has it automates the assembly of furniture using coded indica which saves time and cost for manufactures.
Regarding Dependent claim 2, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses wherein the camera is further configured to scan the part to determine dimensions of the part (see col 60, lines 3-5, discloses that the indica provide dimensional disposition data associated with a part).
Regarding Dependent claim 3, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses wherein the instructions provided by the barcode include co-ordinates on the part for applying the adhesive or attaching the first hardware component (see col 60, lines 3-5 & fig. 10G, discloses that the indica provide data associated with coordinates on the part to perform the assembly instructions).
Regarding Dependent claim 4, with dependency of claim 1, Chen mentions in col. 2, lines 65-67 the application of adhesives for attaching the indica, but fails to teach the robot applying any adhesive to furniture parts. Shinozaki discloses wherein the processor is configured to determine a position on the part to apply the adhesive based on the instructions provided by the barcode (see abstract); Shinozaki fails to teach any assembly of furniture parts using the robot. Ross discloses that applying Autonomous robots for the purpose of furniture parts assembly is well known (see pg. 855, paragraphs 1-4). It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented known techniques for applying adhesive for furniture assembly using the robot, has it automates the assembly of furniture using coded indica which saves time and cost for manufactures.
Regarding Dependent claim 5, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses wherein the processor is configured to determine the position on the part to attach the first hardware component based on the instructions provided by the barcode (see col 60, lines 3-5, discloses that the indica provide dimensional disposition data associated with a part).
Regarding Dependent claim 6, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses wherein the gripping mechanism is a pair of parallel plates (see fig. 1).
Regarding Dependent claim 7, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including hinge mounting plate used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including hinge mounting plate that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 8, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including hinge mounting plate from a hardware provider used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including hinge mounting plate that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 9, with dependency of claim 1, Chen discloses in fig. 1, a single robotic gripping arm. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have implemented multiple varieties of robot configurations for performing an assembly that includes a second gripping mechanisms to grip parts has it provides more control and saves additional time.
Regarding Dependent claim 10, with dependency of claim 9, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including slide and slide spacer used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including a slide and slide spacer that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 12, with dependency of claim 1, Chen mentions in col. 2, lines 65-67 the application of adhesives for attaching the indica, but fails to teach the robot applying any adhesive to furniture parts. Shinozaki discloses wherein the multi-functional robotic head further comprises a second applicator mechanism configured to apply a third hardware component to the part (see abstract); Shinozaki fails to teach any assembly of furniture parts using the robot. Ross discloses that applying Autonomous robots for the purpose of furniture parts assembly is well known (see pg. 855, paragraphs 1-4). It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented known techniques for applying adhesive for furniture assembly using the robot, has it automates the assembly of furniture using coded indica which saves time and cost for manufactures.
10.	Claims 16, 20-21 and 23-28 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Chen (U.S. 4,613,942, filed Oct. 22, 1984) in view of Ross (NPL- IkeaBot: An Autonomous Multi-Robot Coordinated Furniture Assembly System, published May 2013, pgs. 855-862).
Regarding Independent claim 16, Chen discloses A method of assembling a piece of furniture with a robot, the method comprising:
scanning a barcode on a part by the robot, the barcode providing instructions to the robot for attaching one or more hardware components to the part to assemble the piece of furniture (see fig.1, numeral 14 & col. 2, lines 45-65, discloses a camera for obtaining and processing a coded indica image on a part within its field of vision. Further supporting use of a bar code for the indica in col. 4, lines 35-67. The part is then used to perform an assembly operation by the robot arm has determined by the indica outlined in col. 3, lines 25-35 & abstract);
selecting a first hardware component to attach to the part by the robot, the first hardware component selected based on the instructions provided to the robot (see col. 5, lines 5-20, discloses parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached thereby applying fasteners for assembly);
manoeuvring the first hardware component to a first position of the part to be attached to the part, the first position of the part determined by the robot based on the instructions provided to the robot (see fig. 1 & col. 5, lines 5-20, discloses using a computer that communicates with the robotic arm and manipulator to receive instructions from the camera that obtained the indica image that is decoded to provide assemble instruction to the robot); and
attaching the first hardware component to the part by the robot to assemble the piece of furniture (see fig. 1 & col. 5, lines 5-20, discloses using a computer that communicates with the robotic arm and manipulator to receive instructions from the camera that obtained the indica image that is decoded to provide assemble instruction to the robot). Chen discloses obtaining robot assembly operation instructions based on captured indica placed on a part, he fails to teach that parts are used for the assembly of furniture. Ross discloses that applying Autonomous robots for the purpose of furniture parts assembly is well known (see pg. 855, paragraphs 1-4). It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented known techniques for furniture assembly using the robot, has it automates the assembly of furniture using coded indica which saves time and cost for manufactures.
Regarding Dependent claim 20, with dependency of claim 16, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including hinge mounting plate used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including hinge mounting plate that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 21, with dependency of claim 20, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including hinge mounting plate from a storage location used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including hinge mounting plate that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 23, with dependency of claim 21, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including slide and slide spacer used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including a slide and slide spacer that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 24, with dependency of claim 23, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including slide and slide spacer from a storage location used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including a slide and slide spacer that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
Regarding Dependent claim 25, with dependency of claim 24, Chen discloses manoeuvring the second hardware component to a second position to be attached to the part, the second position determined by the robot based on the instructions provided to the robot (see fig.1, numeral 14 & col. 2, lines 45-65, including the explanation provided in the independent claim).
Regarding Dependent claim 26, with dependency of claim 25, Chen discloses attaching the second hardware component to the part by the robot (see fig.1, numeral 14 & col. 2, lines 45-65, including the explanation provided in the independent claim).
Regarding Dependent claim 27, with dependency of claim 26, Chen discloses after attaching the second hardware component to the part by the robot, selecting a third hardware component to attach to the part (see fig.1, numeral 14 & col. 2, lines 45-65, including the explanation provided in the independent claim).
Regarding Dependent claim 28, with dependency of claim 27, Chen discloses in col. 5, lines 5- 15 that parts can also include assembly components such as screws or bolts that are to be attached. He fails to teach a list of all hardware components including an adjustable shelf bracket used for assembly. It would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the application to have supplemented any number of hardware components including an adjustable shelf bracket that could be used in assembly to which an indica can be affixed, has it provides robot manipulation to a broad array of field applications.
It is noted that any citation [[s]] to specific, pages, columns, lines, or figures in the prior art references and any interpretation of the references should not be considered to be limiting in any way.  A reference is relevant for all it contains and may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill in the art. [[See, MPEP 2123]]
